characters: Habiba: a curious nine-year-old Ghanaian girl wearing a soft peach headscarf and a neat sky-blue cotton dress.
Auntie Gyamea: her warm, attentive Ghanaian aunt wearing a rust-and-gold African-print wrapper cloth, matching headwrap, and plain cream kitchen apron.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious voice for Habiba; a warm, firm voice for Auntie Gyamea
narrationPlan.pace: Careful and clear, firm on the safety rule (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A soft simmering sound with a gentle drum (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Wooden stirring paddles and spoons (such as banku ta or wooden ladles) are everyday essentials in Ghanaian kitchens because wood stays comfortable to hold.
Child burn prevention comes first: children stay back from stoves and test heat conduction only with safe warm tap water.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Verify that the classroom/home activity specifies safe warm tap water or sun-warmed water only—never boiling or hot stove water.
Check the science: metals are good thermal conductors, whereas wood and plastic are thermal insulators.

teacherGuide.overview: A safe household science story comparing thermal conductors (metal) and insulators (wood), linking everyday Ghanaian kitchen tools to material properties and strict stove safety.
learningGoals: Identify which material lets heat pass through easily and which blocks it.
Explain why cooking pots and spoons often have wooden or plastic handles.
State and follow kitchen burn-safety rules.
beforeReading: Show a metal spoon and a wooden spoon and ask: which one stays cooler when stirring warm food, and why?
whileReading: Pause on page 4 so learners can explain where the warmth on the metal handle came from.
afterReading: Test a metal spoon, wooden spoon, and plastic spoon in a cup of safe sun-warmed or warm tap water for five minutes.
Sort classroom and kitchen objects by what material their handles are made of.
discussion: Why are pot bodies made of metal while their handles are often wood or plastic?
Why must children stay away from lit coal pots and gas stoves?
reflection: What is one thing you do at home to help keep younger siblings safe around the cooking area?

support: Sort picture cards of spoons and pots under “warms up fast (metal)” and “stays cool (wood/plastic)”.
stretch: Predict whether a plastic spoon handle will feel like the metal spoon or the wooden spoon, then test it in warm tap water.

culturalNotes: Wooden stirring paddles and spoons (such as banku ta or wooden ladles) are everyday essentials in Ghanaian kitchens because wood stays comfortable to hold.
Child burn prevention comes first: children stay back from stoves and test heat conduction only with safe warm tap water.
localiseThis: Reference familiar wooden paddles and spoons used for porridge, soup, and banku.
Never bring boiling water into a pupil activity; use only safe warm tap or sun-warmed water.

factCheck.claim: Metals conduct heat rapidly along a spoon handle, whereas wood is a poor conductor (thermal insulator) that stays cool.
factCheck.explanation: Metals transfer thermal energy quickly from warm water up the handle, while wood slows heat transfer, making wooden handles safer to hold.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Ghana Primary Integrated Science Curriculum (Heat Energy: Conductors and Insulators)
